https://www.mfa.gov.lv/en/article/baiba-.text: Baiba Braže in Moldova: Latvia will continue to support Moldova’s European integration politically and practically Published: 04.08.2026. Flickr Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs Facebook X / Twitter Linkedin Threads On 3 August 2026, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, met with Moldova’s top officials during a working visit to the country to discuss Moldova’s integration into the European Union, the security situation in the region, the reintegration of Transnistria, support for Ukraine and the expansion of bilateral cooperation between Latvia and Moldova. During the working visit, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, met with the President of Moldova, Maia Sandu; the Prime Minister, Vasile Tofan; and the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mihai Popșoi. During her meeting with Maia Sandu, the Minister discussed the security situation in the region, plans for the reintegration of Transnistria, and Moldova’s progress toward integration into the European Union. “The terms for Transnistria’s reintegration are determined entirely by Moldova itself,” Baiba Braže emphasised. The Minister commended Moldova’s achievements on its path toward the European Union and encouraged consistent continuation of reforms. Latvia supports Moldova’s European integration both politically and practically and advocates the earliest possible opening of all accession negotiation chapters with Moldova and Ukraine. In a conversation with Vasile Tofan, opportunities to expand bilateral cooperation between Latvia and Moldova and to foster closer ties between businesses in both countries were discussed. The officials also discussed the priorities of the government of Moldova, including the continuation of reforms and the strengthening of economic growth. “Latvian companies are interested in cooperating with Moldova, particularly in the fields of information and communications technologies and renewable energy,” the Minister said. As successful examples of cooperation, she cited direct airBaltic flights between Riga and Chișinău, as well as the involvement of Latvian non-governmental organisations, experts and companies in Moldova’s modernisation projects. During her meeting with Mihai Popșoi, Baiba Braže expressed strong support for Moldova’s European integration and discussed further support for Ukraine. “We highly value Moldova’s accession to the Coalition of the Willing. Let us continue working together to achieve a just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” Baiba Braže stated. Latvia also provides Moldova with practical support in strengthening security and stability. Last year, Latvia deployed its first civilian expert to the European Union Partnership Mission in Moldova. Actis-backed Rezolv Energy has secured the final legal approval required to begin construction of its 1.2GW Dama Solar project in Arad County in the west of Romania. The Romanian Energy Regulatory Authority (ANRE) has issued the solar PV project’s setting-up authorisation, following an increase in planned capacity from earlier designs through technological advances and optimisation. According to the firm, the project is set to become the largest solar PV plant in the European Union (EU) once commissioned. Construction is expected to begin after financial close. The project is backed by two contracts for difference (CfDs) awarded by Romania’s Ministry of Energy in the country’s second CfD auction in 2025. Rezolv also plans to install a large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) alongside the solar plant. The project will include an 82-hectare nature reserve, which Rezolv said would be one of the largest private-led nature restoration initiatives associated with a solar project in south-east Europe. Rezolv is currently progressing financing and procurement and expects to reach financial close soon, the company said. The project was acquired from the Monsson Group in 2022 , with the company then expecting it to feature 1.6 million solar panels and generate an average 1,500GWh of electricity annually. Rezolv Energy was launched by Actis in July 2022, with co-investment from Mubadala, to develop renewable energy projects across central and south-east Europe. Headquartered in Prague, the company has a portfolio spanning solar and wind, including the 225MW St. George Solar Park in Bulgaria and two wind projects in Romania. Econergy connects 59MW Iancu Jianu solar project in Romania In other Romanian news, Israel-headquartered independent power producer (IPP) Econergy Renewable Energy has connected its 59MW Iancu Jianu solar PV project to the country’s electricity grid. The project is Econergy’s fifth connected project in Romania, taking its connected and ready-to-connect capacity in the country to 743MW, alongside a further 861MW under construction. The company plans to gradually ramp-up power deliveries. Econergy is also developing a 35MW/70MWh BESS at Iancu Jianu, which is expected to connect to the grid in the second quarter of 2027. The BESS is part of Econergy’s broader strategy to co-locate storage with solar projects, targeting additional revenues from grid balancing, price arbitrage and peak-demand response. Econergy operates across Romania, Italy, Poland, the UK, Germany, Spain and Greece, with a project pipeline of more than 12.5GW. Apart from Romania, its portfolio includes a 52MW operational solar project in Poland, and around 20MW of operational solar capacity in Italy, alongside larger development pipelines in these markets. Last year, Econergy agreed to acquire a 100% stake in the 155MW Ratesti solar project in Romania from Nofar Energy through its subsidiary Econergy International in a €45.6 million (US$52.5 million) transaction. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Eyad Shadid at Sydney’s town hall in Sydney. He is suing NSW police. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian Australian police and policing Palestinian Australian sues NSW police claiming he was punched at Herzog rally when helping prayer group Exclusive : Eyad Shadid launches civil case in district court after charges against him dropped, alleging he was ‘battered’ near Sydney’s town hall in February Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jordyn Beazley Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Palestinian Australian man who alleges he was punched in the face when trying to stop police from harassing Muslim men praying during an anti–Isaac Herzog protest is suing New South Wales over “a series of false accusations”. Eyad Shadid has launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall. The Palestine Action Group member, in his statement of claim, says NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution. “I attended the protest to object to our government rolling out the red carpet for Isaac Herzog , president of a state that has been found by United Nations commissioners and most major human rights organisations to be perpetrating a genocide,” Shadid told Guardian Australia. Footage of police officer boasting about punching Sydney anti-Herzog protester raises questions about conduct Read more “The right to protest in this state must mean more than words on paper and, if we must go to court to prove that, then so be it. I did not go to town hall looking for trouble. I went to be counted.” Shadid, 26, was looking for his mother – who, like his father, is from Palestine – after they became separated during the protest on the evening of 9 February. He found himself between a group of Muslim men praying and advancing police when, according to his statement of claim, he told officers: “Stop, they are praying.” Const Daniel Stewart then allegedly dragged Shadid, who had travelled from Parramatta, to the ground and punched him in the face and twisted his wrist. Another officer kneeled on his head, the documents allege. Shadid alleges that when on the ground another officer handcuffed him and he was taken into custody. He was charged with failing to comply with a police direction and resisting arrest. In May, NSW police dropped the charges. Since then, three others charged after the protest have had their charges withdrawn. More than 20 protesters are due to face a joint trial in mid-2027. View image in fullscreen Eyad Shadid returns to Sydney’s town hall. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian Shadid alleges in court documents that Stewart failed to tell another officer deciding whether to charge him that the police line had been advancing towards people praying – and he’d requested the police stop because of that. He claimed the omission was “deliberate” and that Stewart falsely alleged Shadid threatened him with words to the effect of: “Mate, I’d fuckin’ drop you.” In his police statement, Stewart wrote the group of men “began” to pray as the police line moved forward and he was acting in the lawful execution of his duty when he arrested Shadid. Shadid claims that allegation was “dishonest” and designed to make it look like the prayer was a “cynical ploy” to frustrate officers. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email NSW police issued a statement three days after the protest confirming the prayer had been authorised, but claimed that message was not passed on to officers . The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, apologised “for any offence that may have been taken” after officers dragged away those praying. After Shadid’s charges were dropped, the police prosecutor agreed officers had not given him a move-on direction. The 26-year-old was awarded costs. “As a consequence of the matters pleaded herein, the plaintiff was assaulted, battered, falsely imprisoned, subjected to a misfeasance in public office, and maliciously prosecuted,” his statement of claim argues. Shadid, a social services worker, is seeking aggravated and exemplary damages, arguing there was an “oppressive abuse of police powers” and he was prosecuted for “exercising a lawful democratic right to engage in peaceful protest”. Shadid said after he was charged his name was published in media reports and he lost business clients. View image in fullscreen Eyad Shadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian Shadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna, said the case involved “very troubling allegations of police misconduct”. “We claim that Mr Shadid was violently assaulted and arrested without any lawful basis and then charged and prosecuted on the basis of a series of false accusations and misleading omissions,” Hanna said. The defence is yet to file its response to Shadid’s statement of claim. The NSW premier, Chris Minns , and NSW police declined to comment while the matter was before the court. Minns said after the rally that police were “put in an impossible situation” after protesters attempted to defy the public assembly restriction declaration (Pard) law. He refused to apologise to the prayer group or for the police’s conduct. In April, the state’s court of appeal found that law unconstitutional, ruling in favour of the Palestine Action Group and Blak Caucus. Derek Jones, who became known as “white shirt guy” , said in May he intended to launch legal action in the supreme court against police regarding their conduct at the Herzog rally. “It was completely unprovoked, unwarranted, excessive, crazy,” the 56-year-old finance worker told Guardian Australia at the time. The February protest is the subject of a police watchdog investigation after allegations of widespread police brutality. Footage emerged earlier this week of a separate incident in which an officer boasted about punching a protester. The police commissioner, when asked about the video on Wednesday, said: “The language is something that I don’t condone, but I need to understand the context of it.” Herzog was invited to Australia by the federal government after the antisemitic massacre in Bondi when 15 people were killed by two allegedly Islamic State-inspired gunmen. The resulting claims shed light on Xbox 's place in Microsoft's H2 2026 priorities, while also identifying the exact threshold where the service formerly known as xCloud supposedly starts losing money. Microsoft announced the incoming Xbox Cloud Gaming limits on September 3, with the changes scheduled to take effect in November, just over six years after cloud gaming joined Game Pass Ultimate on September 15, 2020. The new monthly allowances are 15 hours for Ultimate, 10 for Premium, and five for Essential, with subscribers able to purchase additional cloud time after reaching their limit. Microsoft has yet to reveal the pricing of those top-ups and estimates that the change will affect roughly 4% of Game Pass subscribers. The company has since softened the rollout for some existing users in select markets by offering limited grandfathering guarantees, though the broader policy remains in place. Posts By Dominik Bošnjak Xbox Cloud Gaming Reportedly Loses Money After Merely 15 Hours of Streaming a Month The Controversial Monthly Usage Cap Did Not Come Out of Nowhere Close A composite image featuring a fluorescent Xbox Cloud Gaming logo superimposed on silhouettes of a notebook, tablet, smartphone, and an Xbox Wireless controller on a dark green background. The shadows in the image were flattened to an "Eerie Black" shade. Xbox Cloud Gaming Keyboard Mouse Setup is shown. A September 5 Windows Central report from longtime Microsoft insider Jez Corden claims Xbox Cloud Gaming effectively starts losing money once a subscriber exceeds 15 hours of monthly use, citing unnamed company officials familiar with the matter. According to his sources, the 15-hour threshold is driven by the ongoing AI boom and its ever-growing compute demands. Azure server rack space allocated to workloads other than AI is therefore becoming increasingly difficult to justify internally, the same sources said. That explanation goes considerably further than Microsoft's official position that cloud gaming simply becomes more expensive as users play more and for longer periods. The report does not necessarily mean Microsoft is replacing Xbox cloud hardware with AI servers. Corden said the servers can run AI workloads off-peak but are not optimized for them, pointing instead to the opportunity cost of using data center capacity for gaming as AI demand surges. Microsoft’s latest earnings support that view: Azure demand still exceeds supply despite 31 new data centers and another gigawatt of capacity added in fiscal Q4, when capital expenditures hit $41 billion. The pressure comes as cloud gaming usage rose 45% year-over-year in December 2025 and Microsoft expanded support for streaming games users already own . Some recurring subscribers in Australia, Brazil, and Poland will reportedly keep unlimited streaming for now, while U.S. notices confirm the caps will apply there, making this limited regional grandfathering rather than a policy reversal. The change comes as Xbox CEO Asha Sharma seeks to recover from earlier Game Pass pricing decisions, saying acquisitions and retention improved after subscription price cuts in spring 2026. Sharma nevertheless says Xbox expects to return to growth by the end of FY2027 . Microsoft has also left room for further cloud gaming changes and has yet to announce several key details concerning the controversial November 2026 overhaul, top-up pricing being chief among them.
